summary.text:
A strategy paper worth reading twice, and the strongest reconciliation the library has recorded on a forward-looking paper. Our file at 31 March 2026 holds 41 PWLB loans totalling £239,382,618 at a weighted 4.4717%, against Oxfordshire's paragraph 13 opening balance of £239.383m at 4.470% — match to the penny on principal and to the basis point on rate.

The most distinctive passage is paragraph 28. The TMST has agreed that if a new proposed rate on a LOBO call is higher than the equivalent PWLB certainty rate, the default position is to repay without penalty — a mechanical rule tied to a number we publish daily. Two £5m LOBOs have calls in 2026/27, one with two options in year and one with a single, so three test events on £10m of debt against a live-number trigger. No other council in the library has printed the trigger in advance in this form; the pattern elsewhere (Wolverhampton three refused, Newcastle £81m of options, Dexia calling at Kent and Tameside inside the same window) is decisions taken at each call rather than a rule set in advance. LOBO share fell from 16.6% to 7.6% over 2025/26 — not decomposed in the paper.

The rate forecast is dated and testable. The Executive Summary hedged 3.75% or 3.50% for the start of 2026/27 reducing to 3.25% by year end; Arlingclose's central case (Annex 1) took Bank Rate to 3.25% by Sep-26 and held it, with 20y gilt central falling 4.85% at Mar-26 to 4.75% by Sep-26. Six months in the higher of the two figures is where Bank Rate sits, and the OIS curve on the 14 August PM fixing prices 4.11% at one year — market above the paper's central and moving away from it. 20y PWLB certainty at 6.38% is 78bp above the 5.60% top of the paper's own medium-term borrowing range in paragraph 20. Internal borrowing is forecast at £295m for 2026/27 against a £300m maximum (paragraph 32) — £5m under the wall — and the long-term lending limit steps down from £150m in 2026/27 to £80m by 2030/31 as cash draws down, with a -£160m Unusable DSG Reserve helping drive that draw.

The CFR is not printed in the text — Prudence and Affordability indicators sit in the separate Capital & Investment Strategy paper (paragraph 30) and CFR appears only on the p6 chart. Balance-sheet identity cannot be closed to the pound: £264m external + £295m internal = £559m is consistent with a chart CFR near £600m and c£40m of other long-term liabilities, but not text-verifiable. Contact officer Tim Chapple named on the front sheet with address; Head of Corporate Finance Kathy Wilcox cleared the comments and has an address at paragraph 80.

officer.subject: Your paragraph 28 LOBO rule, and the three calls this year
officer.body:
Hi Tim,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since a strategy was set. So below are a few thoughts on your February strategy read six months in, ahead of the next quarterly treasury report to Audit and Governance. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paragraph 28 is the clearest LOBO policy statement we've read anywhere, which is what most of what follows is about.

The cross-check first: our file has 41 PWLB loans totalling £239,382,618 at 4.4717% weighted, against the £239.383m at 4.470% in your paragraph 13. Match to the penny on principal and to the basis point on rate — the strongest reconciliation we've seen on a strategy paper.

The line that reads sharpest is paragraph 28 itself: the TMST has agreed that if a new proposed rate on a LOBO call is higher than the equivalent PWLB certainty rate, the default position is to repay without penalty. That's the sentence a member reads and immediately understands. Two £5m LOBOs have calls in 2026/27, one with two options in year and one with a single, so three test events on £10m of debt against a rule that turns on a number we publish daily — the certainty curve, at both the 10:30 and 14:00 fixings. Every council's book gets priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, so the second half of any lender proposal — the without-penalty part — is a page rather than a piece of work.

For context on how distinctive that rule is: of the councils we've read this year, Wolverhampton has three LOBO calls already refused, Newcastle has £81m of LOBO options outstanding against a 3.15% budget assumption, and Dexia called at both Kent and Tameside inside a single window this summer. Every one of those was a decision taken at the time. Oxfordshire is the only council we've read that has printed the trigger in advance and made it mechanical.

The other reading, dated and testable in a way most strategies aren't, is your rate forecast. The Executive Summary hedged 3.75% or 3.50% at year start reducing to 3.25% by year end, and Arlingclose's central case in Annex 1 took Bank Rate to 3.25% by Sep-26 and held it there. Six months in, Bank Rate is 3.75% — the higher of your two — and the OIS curve on the 14 August PM fixing prices 4.11% at one year, so the market is above the strategy's central case and moving away from it. On the long end 20y PWLB certainty is 6.38%, about 78bp above the top of your 4.60-5.60% medium-term borrowing range in paragraph 20. That doesn't change the paragraph 66 case for internal borrowing while cash lasts — the £10.30m in-house interest receivable more than covers the £13.04m external interest payable when the £3.34m external-fund dividends are added — but it changes what an external roll would price at.

Which brings the last thread. Paragraph 32 puts internal borrowing at £295m for 2026/27 against a £300m maximum — £5m under the wall — and paragraph 7 steps the long-term lending limit from £150m in 2026/27 down to £80m by 2030/31, matching the cash drawdown that a -£160m Unusable DSG Reserve helps drive. The interactive liability benchmark pathway at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is live-data and lets you stress the year the internal position stops being available; with CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates it becomes central for everyone. The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve; July's sector activity was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers averaging 5.02%, so you can see how much appetite is there before you need it rather than after.

On training, three fit Oxfordshire: LOBOs and lender options, for the paragraph 28 rule and the three calls; Cost of carry and internal borrowing, for the paragraph 66 strategy behind £295m of it; and Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, for the £295m/£300m position and the lending-limit descent. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this reports into. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.
